newsitem.title: GERMANY: FORECAST - German M3 to slow but prompt no rate cut.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - German M3 to slow but prompt no rate cut.

text.p: German M3 money supply growth likely slowed in September after accelerating slightly in August, but this will not prompt the central bank to lower interest rates in the near term, analysts said on Friday.

Economists estimate M3 money supply, which foreshadows inflation developments, grew at an annualised rate of between 8.2 and 8.5 percent in September, down from August's 8.7 percent rate. In July, the growth rate was 8.6 percent.

M3 money supply comprises cash in circulation, time, sight and short-term savings deposits and the headline figure measures growth as compared with the average growth rate of the fourth quarter of the year earlier.
The data is expected to be released early next week.
But a slowdown in M3 growth will not prompt the Bundesbank to nudge interest rates lower now because the economy is recovering, economists said.

Economists agreed the slight uptick in August M3 growth was a one-off development, unlikely to derail a trend of slowing growth rates but they did not see eye to eye on the size of the slowdown in September.

All said the relatively large liquidity overhang which helped fuel August M3 growth was no longer a key factor for the September figure and its absence would automatically contribute to the expected slowdown.
"We expect that the liquidity overhang was not there anymore at the end of August, and that will have helped slow growth," Mathias Haffner, economist at BZW in Frankfurt said.

Some economists added that the shift of money from bank deposits into shares and bonds -- a process known as money capital formation which slows down money supply growth -- picked up in September after being worryingly weak in recent months.
Haffner predicted that dissipating fears about Europe's planned currency union may have whetted investor appetites for longer-dated securities again.
Offsetting the positive effect of an expected increase in money capital formation however will be ongoing strong lending to the private sector, economists said.

Recent data have not pointed to any slowdown in economic growth, leading economists to expect the trend of strong lending, growing at a seasonally adjusted average rate of seven percent over the last six months, will remain unbroken in September.
At the same time some economists admitted Bundesbank officials had dampened hopes for a much lower headline M3 figure.
The central bank's chief economist, Otmar Issing, on Thursday said M3 growth would probably not slow enough to reach the four-to-seven percent target corridor this year.
"After Issing hinted that M3 was unlikely to reach its goal this year, we expect the number will not show such a big drop," said Eckhard Schulte, economist at Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt.
But regardless of what the number will actually be, economists and analysts predicted the Bundesbank would not react by nudging interest rates lower again.

"There is simply no reason to cut interest rates again at this time," said Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel-Bank bond market analyst Florian Staerk, adding that the economy was performing so well that a rate cut now may even be dangerous by fuelling inflationary pressures.

The Bundesbank in August surprised markets by slashing its main money market rate by a hefty 30 basis points to three percent and has since said there was no need to act again in the immediate future.
Consequently even the bond markets are unlikely to receive September's M3 number with great interest. "The number will be totally irrelevant," IBJ's Schulte said.
